chapters.title: The Elements of Behavior
chapters.hook: A habit you cannot keep is not a willpower problem, it is a missing piece, and there are only three pieces to check.
chapters.counterintuition: Most readers assume a failed habit means they did not want it badly enough. Fogg's claim is that wanting it more is almost never the fix. The behavior failed because motivation, ability, or a prompt was missing at the moment it should have fired, and only one of those three is a reliable lever.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a behavior you meant to do did not happen, walk back to that moment and ask one question: was wanting missing, was the action too big, or did nothing cue you right then?

breakdown.fastRead:
You meant to drink more water today. You did not. The bottle is right there, half full, sitting on the desk where you left it Monday.

A behavior happens when three pieces line up at once. You want it. You can do it right now. Something in the moment points at it. Pull one out and nothing happens. Most days the missing piece is not your willpower. It is the cue, or the size of the ask.

You are not lazy. You are under-designed. Before you reach for a verdict, ask which of the three was missing and fix that one. Leave the other two alone.
breakdown.deepRead:
A retired electrician keeps a blood-pressure cuff in a drawer he never opens. His cardiologist wants a daily reading. He wants to give her one. The cuff stays in the drawer.

Notice what is not the problem. He is not unmotivated. He knows how the cuff works. He just has no moment in his morning that touches that drawer. Nothing in his day points at the cuff.

A behavior lands when three pieces meet at the same instant. You want to do it. You can do it right now, with the energy you actually have. And something cues you right then, so the wanting and the doing meet. Pull any one out and nothing happens, no matter how good a person you are.

Most of us reach for motivation first. We try to want it more. We make a vow on Sunday night. By Thursday the vow is thin and we feel like we failed at being a person. You did not fail at being a person. You failed at design.

Move the cuff next to the coffee tin. The next morning he reaches for coffee, sees the cuff, takes the reading. Same man, same week, different result. The cue was the missing piece the whole time, and the fix took ten seconds and one rearranged drawer. His cardiologist gets her numbers. His heart gets watched.

So when something you meant to do did not happen, walk back to the exact moment it should have. Ask one question. Was the wanting missing, was the action too big for the moment you had, or did nothing point at it? One will raise its hand. Fix that one. Leave the other two alone.
breakdown.fullRead:
On a Tuesday afternoon a junior associate at a small law firm stares at a leather notebook on her nightstand. She bought it two weeks ago to write three lines before bed. Three lines. She has done it twice.

Walk the week with her. Monday she was lit up. New notebook, fresh pen, tomorrow we become the kind of person who reflects. Tuesday she did it, and felt a small flicker of pride before sleep. That flicker is the wiring happening. Wednesday a deposition ran late and she fell into bed in her clothes. Thursday the notebook felt like a small accusation. By Sunday she was deciding whether she was, deep down, the type of person who finishes things.

She is not the problem. The design is. She built the whole habit on top of motivation, and motivation is a tide. It comes in, it goes out, and you cannot build a house on it. When Monday's wave went back out there was nothing else holding the behavior up. No anchor in her routine. No version small enough to do at 11:48 p.m. with mascara still on.

Carry this lens with you. Any behavior, any one, only happens when three pieces arrive together. You have to want to do it. You have to be able to do it right now, with the energy and time you actually have. And something has to point at it in the moment, so the wanting and the doing meet on a real Tuesday. Want, can, cue. Miss any one and nothing happens, and your character has nothing to do with it.

So when something you meant to do did not happen, do not start with who you are. Start with what was missing. Walk back to the exact moment it should have happened and ask which of the three was absent.

A night-shift nurse cannot keep up her water intake on twelve-hour rotations. She wants to. She is perfectly able to lift a bottle to her mouth. What broke? The cue. Her old reminder was a desk she used to sit at. Now she walks past it once a shift. Her body is not the issue. Her cue is in the wrong building.

A freelance illustrator picks an eight-minute wrist routine to protect a wrist that pays her rent. She does it twice. She quits. She is not weak. Eight minutes between commissions, when her hands are warm and a client is waiting, is too much. The wanting is there. The cue is there, every time she stops drawing. Ability is what is missing. If she does not fix it, her wrist gives out and rent gets harder. The fix is not more grit. Two stretches, thirty seconds, done.

Notice what this asks of you. Not more virtue. A short pause and one honest question. Was I unmotivated, was the action too big for the moment I had, or did nothing in my day point at it? Whichever one raises its hand is the one you redesign. Leave the other two alone.

The miss is not a verdict on your soul. It is information. Something was missing at 7:14 a.m. or 10:30 p.m. or right after the bus pulled away. Find that something. Put it back.

examples.title: Ingegerd's Water Bottle Sits Full at 4 a.m.

planSpec.domain: a night-shift nurse trying to drink more water during twelve-hour rotations
planSpec.audience: a healthcare worker whose schedule wrecks ordinary routines
planSpec.stakes: chronic dehydration headaches that bleed into patient handoffs
planSpec.requiredBeat: she traces her failed water-bottle habit to a missing prompt rather than weak willpower, and decides to redesign the cue instead of trying harder

examples.scenario: It is 4:12 a.m. on the cardiac stepdown floor, and Ingegerd, ten hours into her shift, finds her water bottle on the med cart exactly where she set it at 6 p.m. Still full. Her temples are pulsing the dull ache she now associates with a botched handoff at seven. She has tried sticky notes, a phone alarm she silences without seeing, and a pep talk in the bathroom mirror. The bottle is right there. She is about to write tonight off as another willpower failure. Her hand is on the cap. She has to decide whether the problem is that she does not want it enough, or that nothing in her shift is telling her to drink.
examples.whatToDo: Stop adding willpower. Pick one thing that already happens every hour on the floor (charting a vital, scanning a wristband) and pair the sip to it: after I scan, I drink once.
examples.whyItMatters: Behavior needs a cue at the moment of action. Trying harder cannot create a prompt that the environment is not already firing, so the fix is to attach the sip to a signal that the shift itself produces.

examples.title: Stanislas Moves the Blood-Pressure Cuff Next to the Coffee Tin

planSpec.domain: a retired electrician learning to take a daily blood-pressure reading at his kitchen counter
planSpec.audience: an older adult navigating a new medical instruction
planSpec.stakes: whether his cardiologist has data to adjust medication before his next appointment
planSpec.requiredBeat: the cuff sits in a drawer because nothing in his morning routine touches that drawer; the scene shows him moving it next to the coffee tin and a reading happening the next day

examples.scenario: The cuff has lived in the bottom drawer for eleven days, under a stack of warranty cards and a flashlight. Stanislas, sixty-eight, retired from forty years of pulling wire, opens that drawer maybe twice a year. Each morning he scoops coffee from the tin on the counter, reads the paper, forgets the cuff exists. On Tuesday evening he carries the cuff out of the drawer and sets it beside the coffee tin. Wednesday at 7:14 a.m., he scoops, sees the cuff, sits down, and takes a reading.
examples.whatToDo: Move the cuff out of the drawer and place it physically touching something your morning hands already touch. Let the existing routine deliver the prompt for you.
examples.whyItMatters: A behavior needs a prompt at the moment it should happen. A cuff in a closed drawer cannot prompt anyone. A cuff resting against the coffee tin is inside a routine that already fires every day.

examples.title: Fern reads back her journal week and sees the wrong lever

planSpec.domain: a junior associate at a regional law firm trying to journal three lines before bed
planSpec.audience: someone who already feels overscheduled
planSpec.stakes: a quiet sense that another self-improvement attempt is about to die
planSpec.requiredBeat: she walks back through the week and identifies that motivation was high on Monday and gone by Thursday, and concludes the design was leaning on the wrong lever

examples.scenario: It is Friday night. Fern, a junior associate at a regional firm, opens the leather notebook her sister gave her and counts the entries from the past week. Monday: a full half page, looping handwriting, three exclamation points. Tuesday: four lines. Wednesday: two lines, scrawled. Thursday: blank. Friday: blank. She had told herself on Sunday that this time she would stick with it. She sits with the pattern. The notebook was on the nightstand all week. The pen was right there. What faded was not access. What faded was the want.
examples.whatToDo: Stop trying to summon Monday's enthusiasm on Thursday. Cut the behavior to one sentence, anchored after toothbrushing, and let ability carry the week instead of motivation.
examples.whyItMatters: Motivation predictably drains across a workweek, so any habit that depends on feeling like doing it will collapse on the day you most need it. Ability is the lever that holds steady.

examples.title: Osman realizes his Sunday call has no anchor

planSpec.domain: a high school orchestra teacher who keeps meaning to call his aging mother on Sunday afternoons
planSpec.audience: an adult navigating family obligation alongside a busy week
planSpec.stakes: the relationship slowly thinning into voicemails
planSpec.requiredBeat: a conversation with a friend over coffee where he realizes the call has no anchor in his Sunday and is competing with everything else for attention

examples.scenario: Osman is sitting across from his friend Lior at a coffee shop on a Tuesday afternoon, stirring a flat white and saying for the third week in a row that he meant to call his mother on Sunday and somehow didn't. Lior asks, plainly, 'What were you doing right before you didn't call her?' Osman opens his mouth and finds he can't answer. Sunday is laundry, lesson plans, a walk, the news, a nap. The call floats above all of it, unattached. Lior sets down the cup and says, 'So when, exactly, is it supposed to happen?'
examples.whatToDo: Pick one fixed Sunday routine you already do (pouring the second coffee, closing the laundry lid) and pin the call to the moment that routine ends. Write it down in that form.
examples.whyItMatters: A call competing with every Sunday hour against vague intent will lose every time. Tying it to a specific completed action gives the behavior a single moment to fire instead of a whole afternoon to drift through.

examples.title: Rosaline's Eight-Minute Wrist Routine That Never Happens

planSpec.domain: a freelance illustrator trying to stretch her wrists between commissions
planSpec.audience: a self-employed creative whose day has no fixed structure
planSpec.stakes: early signs of repetitive strain that could end her income
planSpec.requiredBeat: the reader is asked to predict which of the three elements is failing, then the scene reveals it is ability — the stretch routine she chose takes eight minutes and she will not do eight minutes

examples.scenario: Rosaline is a freelance illustrator finishing a children's book spread at her dining table. Her right wrist has been clicking for two weeks. She has a stretch routine bookmarked on her phone, eight minutes long, with five exercises and a foam roller. Before reading on, predict which of the three is failing: motivation (she knows the strain could end her work), prompt (the ache itself fires every hour), or ability. She closes the laptop, glances at the bookmark, and opens Instagram instead. Eight minutes is too many.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the routine to one wrist circle after you cap your pen. One. If you find yourself doing the other four stretches, that is a bonus, not the assignment.
examples.whyItMatters: Motivation and prompt were both present and still lost to a behavior her tired hands could not afford. Shrinking the ask is the only lever that survives a low-energy moment.

examples.title: Renzo, the 47 bus, and a paperback that finally opens

planSpec.domain: a line cook who wants to start reading non-cookbook books on the bus ride home
planSpec.audience: a service-industry worker decompressing after a shift
planSpec.stakes: a quiet aspiration to feel like a person with interests outside the kitchen
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sits with the recognition that the bus ride is already an anchor and a prompt is already firing — what was missing was making the behavior small enough to start while still smelling like fryer oil

examples.scenario: Renzo sits in the back of the 47 bus with a paperback of Kafka's letters in his apron pocket, bought eight months ago and carried home every shift since. The bus is dark. His hands smell like fryer oil and lemon. The seat itself is the cue, has always been the cue. He is too tired to read for thirty minutes. He has always been too tired to read for thirty minutes. And tonight it finally lands: the bus ride was the doorway all along, and what he had to do was make the asking smaller than his exhaustion.
examples.whatToDo: Open the paperback on the bus and read one sentence. Just one. If you keep going, that is a gift, not the assignment. Close it after that sentence and let a small flicker of done land.
examples.whyItMatters: The bus ride was already a stable anchor and the seat was already prompting him every night. Ability was the missing leg. Shrinking the read to one sentence puts the behavior inside the energy he actually has after a shift.

questions.prompt: A graphic designer keeps a meditation app on her phone and is genuinely interested in trying it, but two weeks in she has not opened it once. Which best explains why the behavior is not happening?
choices: Wanting and being able are not enough on their own; nothing in her day is cueing the app at the moment she could open it.
Her motivation is clearly fake or shallow, since real interest would override any other obstacles she faces.
Meditation apps require a level of focus most beginners do not have, so the behavior is too advanced for her current ability.
questions.explanation: Three elements have to meet at the same instant. She wants to (motivation) and could (ability), but no prompt is firing in her day. Calling her motivation fake misreads the framework, and assuming the app is too hard ignores that she has not even tried it once.

questions.prompt: A dental hygienist bought a daily multivitamin three weeks ago, set it on a high shelf in the pantry, and has taken it twice. She wants to take it and the pill is easy to swallow. What is the soundest first move?
choices: Move the bottle next to her toothbrush so the act of finishing brushing puts the bottle in her hand.
Set a phone reminder labeled 'TAKE VITAMIN' that fires every morning at 7 a.m. so she cannot ignore it.
Try a chewable formulation in case the pill is harder to take than she realized.
questions.explanation: Wanting and ability are fine; the cue is missing. Anchoring the bottle to a routine she already runs (brushing) makes the prompt automatic. A phone alarm adds friction and fights for attention; switching formulations fixes an ability problem that does not exist.

questions.prompt: A new parent decided to do a fifteen-minute lower-back routine every night to deal with stiffness from carrying the baby. After eight days he has done it twice. He has the mat in the bedroom and remembers each night. What likely went wrong?
choices: He needs to set a stronger intention by writing the goal on a sticky note where he can see it before bed.
Fifteen minutes is too large an ask for a person already exhausted at bedtime; the action does not fit the energy he actually has.
The mat in the bedroom is the wrong cue, since bedrooms are for sleeping and his brain associates them with rest.
questions.explanation: He has motivation and a prompt; the action itself is too big for the moment available. Fifteen minutes after a long parenting day is not realistic. Stronger intention is the willpower trap, and the bedroom-cue theory is a stretch when the real bottleneck is size.

questions.prompt: A regional sales rep keeps meaning to send a short Friday recap email to her manager and has missed it four weeks running. She likes her manager and the email would take three minutes. By 5 p.m. Friday she has already left for the weekend. What is the right diagnosis?
choices: She is signaling, even unconsciously, that she does not respect her manager enough to follow through, and needs to confront that.
Three minutes is too small to feel meaningful, so her brain dismisses the task as not worth the context switch.
The recap is not anchored to anything in her Friday, so by the time it could happen she is already out the door.
questions.explanation: Motivation is fine and the action is small. The cue is the missing piece: nothing in her Friday points at the email before she leaves. Anchoring it to her last meeting or to closing her laptop fixes the design. The respect framing is the shame trap, and 'too small' is the opposite mistake.

questions.prompt: A construction estimator wants to start a habit of reviewing one bid metric each morning. He has the dashboard bookmarked, finds the data interesting, and starts work at his desk every weekday with coffee in hand. Which move is most likely to make this happen tomorrow?
choices: Set a recurring 9 a.m. calendar block titled 'review one metric' so it shows up alongside his other meetings.
Tell two coworkers about the goal so social accountability keeps him honest when motivation dips.
Pin the dashboard tab so it opens automatically when he starts his browser, right as he sits down with coffee.
questions.explanation: All three elements line up best when the dashboard appears at the moment he already runs (sitting down with coffee). Calendar blocks add a competing prompt that is easy to dismiss. Social pressure leans on motivation, which is not the missing piece here.

questions.prompt: A community college librarian planned to do five squats every time she finished her lunch. Week one: did them three days, felt great. Week two: did them once. Week three: not at all. Same lunch routine throughout. Where should she look first?
choices: Motivation faded, so she should reconnect to why squats matter to her overall health goals.
The cue worked once, then went stale; finishing lunch may not be a sharp enough moment to act on.
Five squats is too few to feel worth doing, and her brain stopped registering it as a real task.
questions.explanation: The pattern (worked then faded) signals the prompt is not robust. 'Finishing lunch' is fuzzy with no clear instant. Sharpening the anchor (after I drop my fork) gives the cue an edge. The other diagnoses lead back to willpower or contradict starting tiny.

questions.prompt: A landscaper put sunscreen in his truck, plans to apply it before each job, and knows skin cancer runs in his family. After a month, the bottle has barely been used. He gets in the truck, starts the engine, and drives off. Which element is the weakest link?
choices: The prompt: starting the engine and getting on the road does not pass through the bottle.
The motivation: family history alone is not specific enough to drive a daily action.
The ability: applying sunscreen properly takes a few minutes he does not budget for.
questions.explanation: Motivation is real (family history) and the action is small. The truck routine never touches the sunscreen, so no cue fires at the right moment. Putting the bottle on the steering wheel or next to the keys solves it. The other diagnoses lead toward willpower or overestimate the friction.

questions.prompt: An accountant who wants to switch from afternoon coffee to herbal tea has tried for three weeks. The kettle and tea sit on the counter next to the coffee maker. He sees them every afternoon. He still pours coffee. What is most likely happening?
choices: He is not actually motivated to switch and is fooling himself about wanting a healthier afternoon.
The cue and ability are fine, but the new behavior is competing against a stronger established prompt that already wins.
The kettle is too slow compared to the coffee maker, so ability is the real bottleneck during a busy afternoon.
questions.explanation: The tea has all three elements, but the coffee routine is a stronger, older prompt-and-action chain that fires first. Moving coffee out of sight or anchoring tea to a different earlier moment is the design fix. Doubting motivation is the shame trap; kettle speed is a red herring.

questions.prompt: A delivery driver wants to floss daily. He has been trying for two months. Floss sits on the bathroom counter. He brushes twice a day. He flossed maybe ten times total. Which proposed fix is the soundest?
choices: Read an article on gum disease each Sunday so he stays scared enough to follow through during the week.
Replace nightly brushing with flossing-then-brushing for the next thirty days to force the new behavior.
Floss only one tooth right after he picks up the toothbrush, then brush as usual.
questions.explanation: The cue (picking up the brush) already fires daily. The bottleneck is ability: full flossing is too big a leap. Shrinking the action to one tooth makes it land. Fear-based reading leans on motivation that fades. Replacing brushing creates a new design problem instead of solving the existing one.

reviewCards.front: You promised yourself you would meditate every morning. Two weeks in, it has happened twice. What is the one question to ask before trying again?
reviewCards.back: Walk back to the exact moment it should have happened and ask which of the three was missing: the wanting, the ability given the energy you actually had, or a cue pointing at it right then. One will raise its hand. Fix that one and leave the other two alone.

reviewCards.front: A coworker says she keeps meaning to take a short walk at lunch but never does. Motivation is high, she has the time, she has good shoes by the door. What should you ask her next?
reviewCards.back: Ask what in her workday actually points at the walk at the moment lunch begins. If nothing cues the behavior right then, the prompt is missing, and adding willpower will not fix a missing cue. Tie the walk to something her day already does, like closing her laptop or finishing a specific meeting.

reviewCards.front: You vowed Sunday night to do a forty minute yoga flow every evening. By Thursday it has not happened once, even though you still want it. Which lever is the design leaning on, and which one should it lean on instead?
reviewCards.back: The design is leaning on motivation, which fades by midweek, and on ability, since forty minutes is too big for a tired Thursday. Shrink the behavior until it fits the energy you actually have on the worst night, then anchor it to a moment that already happens, so motivation barely matters.

reviewCards.front: A friend tells you he wants to call his mother on Sundays but keeps forgetting until Monday morning guilt hits. He loves his mother. He has a phone. What is the move?
reviewCards.back: The wanting is there and the ability is there, so the missing piece is a prompt. Anchor the call to something his Sunday already reliably does, such as after he pours his afternoon coffee or right when he sits down after the grocery run, so the cue and the wanting meet at the same instant.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Behavior triage. When something you meant to do did not happen, you walk back to the exact moment it should have, and ask which of three pieces was missing: the wanting, the doing, or the cue. You fix only that one, and you leave the other two alone.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a pill bottle, water bottle, or medical device sits unused for three days in a row, then move it physically into the line of sight of something you already touch every morning, and check tomorrow whether the cue alone fixed it.

If you notice a recurring task slipping past you on Thursdays after a strong Monday start, then stop trying to want it more, and instead attach it to a fixed event already on your calendar (a standup, a lunch, a status email).

If a person you love keeps drifting to voicemail, then pick one weekly thing you already do without fail (Sunday grocery run, Friday last coffee), and make the call the thing you do during it, not after it.

If a new routine takes more than two minutes to start, then cut it down to a thirty-second version before you blame yourself for skipping it, because the size of the behavior was the problem, not your character.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one habit you have failed at in the last month. Tonight, write down the exact moment it should have happened yesterday, and circle which of the three was missing: wanting, doing, or cue. Then make one physical change in your kitchen or bag that fixes only that piece.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, on a quiet evening, list two or three behaviors you meant to do and did not. For each one, name the missing piece in a single word and write the smallest design fix next to it. Keep the list somewhere you will see it the following week, so you can check whether the fix held.

memorableLines.text: You are not lazy. You are under-designed.
memorableLines.why: In six words, it reframes the shame of failed habits as a design problem rather than a character flaw, offering diagnosis where readers expect judgment—surprising and liberating.

memorableLines.text: She built the whole habit on top of motivation, and motivation is a tide. It comes in, it goes out, and you cannot build a house on it.
memorableLines.why: The tide-and-house metaphor is concrete and poetic, explaining why motivation-dependent habits inevitably fail; stands alone without chapter context because the image does the work.

memorableLines.text: You did not fail at being a person. You failed at design.
memorableLines.why: It splits the failure verdict in half—separating self from system—in two parallel clauses that flip the reader's internal narrative from shame to solvability.

chapters.title: Motivation-Focus on Matching
chapters.hook: Motivation is a tide. You cannot build a house on it, so build a house that fits the lowest water mark.
chapters.counterintuition: Most readers assume the fix for a stalled habit is to want it more. The opposite move works better: keep your motivation exactly where it is, and shrink the behavior until it fits your worst Tuesday, not your best Sunday.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Motivation rises and falls like a tide, so size the behavior to your tired-Wednesday floor, not your Sunday-morning ceiling, and the habit survives the low days.

breakdown.fastRead:
It's 3:14 a.m. A nurse pulls up a 20-minute stretching video on her phone. Her back is screaming. She watches none of it. Not that night, not the next. By Friday she can barely lift the laundry basket.

You are not lazy. You are under-designed. The plan got written by Sunday-afternoon you, fresh notebook, clear head. Then Wednesday-night you tried to do it.

Match the behavior to the motivation you have on your worst night, not your best. If two pushups feels like too much, do one. If one feels like too much, do half. Shrink it until your tired self cannot say no. Make it smaller than your bad mood.
breakdown.deepRead:
A high school band director walks to his car at 9:47 p.m., trumpet case in one hand, stack of sheet music in the other. He promised himself one paragraph of journaling after every rehearsal. He skips nine nights in a row.

He tries something smaller. One sentence on a sticky note before the trumpet goes in the case. "Trombones rushed bar 12 again." That is it. He does it every night for a month. By week three he feels a small flicker of pride when he caps the pen. That feeling is the wiring happening.

What changed? Not his discipline. Not some breakthrough about why teaching matters. He stopped writing the plan for a fresh, well-rested teacher and wrote it for the actual man putting away the trumpet at 9:47 p.m.

Motivation is a tide. It comes in, it goes out, and you cannot build a house on it. Design a habit for high tide and you are designing for maybe three days a week. The other four, the habit dies, and you call yourself weak. You are not weak. You are under-designed.

Here is the move. Look at the size of the behavior, then look at how much energy you actually have on a Wednesday night, not a Sunday morning. Make it fit the floor, not the ceiling. A freelance illustrator with ADHD wrote herself two rules: thirty minutes on a good morning, one line on a bad one. Both count. Both keep her drawing.

Before you commit to any new habit, ask one question. What is the smallest version of this that tired-Wednesday you would still do? Write that down. That is your starting line, and the starting line is the only line you have to cross.
breakdown.fullRead:
Greg sits at his kitchen table in slippers, holding a cooling cup of coffee. He retired four months ago. He told everyone he would learn Spanish before flying to meet his daughter-in-law's family in October. He pictured an hour of Duolingo every morning, a notebook, flashcards on the fridge.

It is May. He has managed about fourteen scattered sessions. He keeps thinking he just needs to want it more. The flight is in five months and he is rehearsing how to apologize for not trying. Picture his face at that dinner table, hunting for words he never learned. That is what is at stake.

He does not need to want it more. He needs to want it less, and to design for that.

Motivation is a tide. It comes in, it goes out, and on most days it sits somewhere in the middle, distracted by the dishwasher and the news and a tooth that has started to ache. Build a habit on the high tide and you will be standing in mud most mornings, staring at a plan that no longer fits the day in front of you.

Greg does the thing that actually works. He picks one Spanish phrase. He says it out loud before his first sip of coffee. "Buenos días, mi amor." That is the whole recipe. On a good morning, he keeps going for ten minutes. On a bad one, the phrase still gets said. The habit survives both kinds of day, which means it survives, period.

That is matching. The size of the behavior fits the smallest amount of motivation you can plausibly count on. Not the average. Not the hopeful version. The floor.

A couple in Brooklyn worked this out at their kitchen counter on a Sunday night. They had been fighting about cooking together. One of them wanted dinner at home every weeknight, the other kept ordering Thai by 7 p.m. The conversation went in circles until one of them said, gently, "What can the tired versions of us actually pull off?" The answer was one shared task. Chopping the onion together, even if the rest came from a delivery app. Two minutes. That was the floor. From the floor, things grew, including the marriage.

A warehouse shift supervisor doing his own postmortem on three years of failed budgeting attempts noticed something embarrassing. Every plan he had written assumed Sunday-night him, the man with a quiet hour and a finished coffee. None of the plans accounted for Wednesday-night him, the one collapsing onto the couch after a ten-hour shift and an hour of traffic. The failure was not laziness. It was sizing.

Here is where honesty helps. You probably do not have a willpower problem. You have a sizing problem, and the sizing problem feels like a willpower problem because it shows up the same way. You do not do the thing. But the fix is different. You cannot grit your way into a habit that does not fit. You shrink the habit until it does.

So before you commit to anything new, sit with one question. Picture your worst night this week, the one where you got home late and the dog was barking and you just wanted to lie down. What is the version of this habit the worst-night you would still do? Not should do. Would. Write it down in one sentence and tape it where you will see it. Design for that person, and you stop being someone who keeps quitting.

examples.title: Marisela finds the stretch that fits a 3 a.m. kitchen

planSpec.domain: a night-shift ER nurse trying to start a stretching routine after twelve-hour shifts
planSpec.audience: a healthcare worker whose energy is genuinely depleted, not metaphorically
planSpec.stakes: whether her chronic lower-back pain becomes a career-ending injury within two years
planSpec.requiredBeat: she abandons the 20-minute YouTube routine and reframes the problem as 'what stretch can I do while the kettle boils' — the shift from amplifying willpower to shrinking the behavior to fit her real Tuesday-at-3am self

examples.scenario: At 3:14 a.m., Marisela is home from another twelve-hour shift in the ER and her lower back is doing the thing again, the dull seizing that the orthopedist warned her about. The 20-minute YouTube mobility routine is queued on her laptop. It has been queued for eleven nights. She fills the kettle instead, watches the blue ring of flame, and feels her shoulders drop. While the water climbs toward a boil, she rests her palms on the counter and lets her hips hinge back, one slow exhale into the hamstrings.
examples.whatToDo: Close the 20-minute video. Pick one stretch that fits inside the ninety seconds the kettle already takes, and let that be the whole routine on a shift night.
examples.whyItMatters: Motivation at 3 a.m. after twelve hours on her feet is near zero, and zero motivation cannot lift a 20-minute behavior. A 90-second behavior fits under the floor of her real energy, so it actually happens, and a habit that happens beats one that is correct on paper.

examples.title: Desmond, band director, finds the journal that fits a Tuesday

planSpec.domain: a high school band director trying to journal about each rehearsal
planSpec.audience: a working educator with a packed evening
planSpec.stakes: losing the only feedback loop he has for improving his teaching across a 40-student ensemble
planSpec.requiredBeat: the before shows him bargaining with himself to write 'just one paragraph' and skipping for nine days; the after shows him writing one sentence on a sticky note while putting his trumpet in its case, and the reader sees the matching of behavior-size to leftover energy

examples.scenario: Before: Desmond promises himself one paragraph in the leather notebook after each rehearsal. He bargains the paragraph down to three sentences, then skips entirely for nine straight evenings, the notebook still on the passenger seat, blank. After: he tapes a pad of sticky notes to his trumpet case. While the horn settles into its velvet, he writes one sentence. Tonight's reads: 'Trumpets rushed bar 47, try subdividing.' He sticks it inside the case lid and clicks the latches shut.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the journal entry to one sentence written during a movement you already make, like closing the instrument case, instead of carving out fresh evening time.
examples.whyItMatters: Leftover evening energy is a fixed, small quantity. A behavior larger than that quantity will not fire, no matter how valuable the feedback loop is. Shrinking lets it run on the energy that exists.

examples.title: Rohan and Sigrun negotiate the floor of their weeknight cooking plan

planSpec.domain: a couple deciding whether to commit to cooking dinner together every weeknight
planSpec.audience: two partners with mismatched schedules
planSpec.stakes: whether the resentment building from takeout-and-screens evenings calcifies into something harder to fix
planSpec.requiredBeat: one partner stops defending the ambitious plan and asks aloud 'what is the version of this we can do on the worst night of the week' — the conversation models matching to the floor of their motivation, not the ceiling

examples.scenario: It is 9:14 on a Tuesday and the takeout containers are still on the counter. Rohan is defending the spreadsheet he made: five themed dinners, shared prep on Sunday, no exceptions. Sigrun, still in scrubs, finally puts down her fork. 'Babe. What is the version of this we can do on the worst night of the week. Not the Sunday-Rohan night. The Wednesday-me-after-a-double night.' He starts to answer, then stops. The spreadsheet is for people they are not.
examples.whatToDo: Redesign the plan around the lowest-motivation night you actually have, not the best one. Pick the smallest shared cooking act that survives a Wednesday double shift.
examples.whyItMatters: A habit sized to your peak motivation fails on every night that is not your peak. Matching to the floor means the behavior repeats, and repetition is what the wiring needs.

examples.title: Soraya Picks the Rule That Survives a Bad Morning

planSpec.domain: a freelance illustrator with ADHD trying to build a daily sketching practice
planSpec.audience: a creative professional whose motivation genuinely fluctuates by the hour
planSpec.stakes: her portfolio stagnates and she loses a recurring client who wants to see range
planSpec.requiredBeat: she chooses between 'sketch for 30 minutes' on a high-motivation morning and 'draw one line' on a low-motivation morning, and the reader watches her pick the rule that survives both kinds of day

examples.scenario: Soraya sits at her drafting table in a converted laundry room in Oakland, 7:14 a.m., the second cup of coffee already cooling. Her sketchbook is open. Yesterday she drew for forty minutes and felt like a working illustrator. Today her brain is static, her ADHD meds have not kicked in, and the recurring client wants three new style samples by Friday. She is about to write a daily rule on the inside cover. Her pen hovers between two sentences: 'Sketch for thirty minutes' and 'Draw one line.' She has to pick the one she will still honor on the worst morning of the month.
examples.whatToDo: Write the rule sized to your lowest-motivation morning, not your best one. Pick 'draw one line.' On good days, more will happen on its own.
examples.whyItMatters: A daily rule only compounds if it survives bad days. A rule scaled to peak motivation breaks on the first low day, and a broken streak resets the wiring you were trying to build.

examples.title: Edmund Sits With The Spanish Hour That Never Arrives

planSpec.domain: a recently retired man who promised himself he would learn Spanish before visiting his daughter-in-law's family
planSpec.audience: a 67-year-old who has the time but not the residual cognitive energy he expected
planSpec.stakes: a real trip in eight months and the relationship with grandchildren he cannot yet talk to
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sits with the gap between his daydreamed self ('an hour of Duolingo every morning') and his actual self, and rewrites the behavior to one phrase before the first sip of coffee — the matching is internal, not technique-driven

examples.scenario: Edmund is sixty-seven, eight months from a trip to meet his daughter-in-law's family in Oaxaca. In the retirement he had pictured, he wakes at six, brews coffee, and sits at the kitchen table with Duolingo for a clean unbroken hour. The actual mornings have him staring at the toaster, knees stiff, brain fogged, the app untouched. He sits with the gap. The picture was made by a younger man who did not yet have these mornings. Before his first sip of coffee, he writes one phrase on the back of a receipt: hola, abuela.
examples.whatToDo: Match the behavior to the man who actually shows up at 6 a.m., not the one in the daydream. Cut the Duolingo hour to one Spanish phrase said aloud before the first sip of coffee.
examples.whyItMatters: The hour-long version assumes residual cognitive energy he no longer has at sixty-seven. A behavior sized to his lowest-motivation morning repeats for eight months. A behavior sized to the fantasy does not survive week one.

examples.title: Reuben Lays Out Four Failed Budgets on the Counter

planSpec.domain: a warehouse shift supervisor who keeps abandoning a budgeting habit
planSpec.audience: a worker with variable income and an exhausting commute
planSpec.stakes: a $4,200 emergency fund he has been trying to build for three years
planSpec.requiredBeat: he reconstructs the last four failed attempts and notices each one assumed his Sunday-night motivation, not his Wednesday-night motivation — the diagnosis names mismatched sizing as the actual failure mode, not laziness

examples.scenario: Reuben spreads four index cards on his kitchen counter, one for each budgeting system he has launched and quit in three years. The pattern stares back. Every plan was built on a Sunday night, when he had slept eight hours and felt like the man he wanted to be. None were built for the Wednesday version of him, walking in at 11:40 p.m. after a double, smelling like cardboard. He had been calling that Wednesday man lazy for three years. He sees now it was a sizing problem.
examples.whatToDo: Redesign the habit for your worst night, not your best. Pick a budgeting move small enough to do at 11:40 p.m. after a double shift, then let Sunday-night you accept it as the whole plan.
examples.whyItMatters: A habit only repeats if it survives your low-energy nights. The motivation you feel when planning is not what you will have when acting, so a plan built for your best self collapses on a normal Wednesday.

questions.prompt: A graphic designer keeps abandoning the 30-minute morning yoga routine she set up during a fresh weekend planning session. Which framing best captures the idea of matching the behavior to the motivation she actually has?
choices: Her willpower is too weak; she needs firmer rules and a stricter morning schedule.
Her behavior is sized for her best mornings; she should shrink it to fit her worst ones.
Her schedule is wrong; she should switch the yoga session to evenings instead.
questions.explanation: When the rule is built for the best version of you, it dies on the worst version. Shrinking the behavior to fit her low-motivation mornings keeps the practice alive. Willpower talk and time-shifting both leave the original size mismatch in place.

questions.prompt: A long-haul truck driver promised himself he would read 20 pages a night at the truck stop. He keeps falling asleep on the page, and after three weeks of mostly skipping he is ready to quit entirely. What is the soundest next move?
choices: Shrink the rule to reading one paragraph before he turns off the cab light.
Set a 9pm reading alarm and use a streak app to hold himself accountable.
Switch to audiobooks so he can listen while driving instead of reading at night.
questions.explanation: One paragraph survives the night he is dead on his feet, which is the actual floor of his energy. A 9pm alarm fights exhaustion with a scheduling tool, and audiobooks swap the activity rather than fixing the size mismatch.

questions.prompt: A new parent with a six-week-old wanted to meditate ten minutes a day, but the night feedings have wrecked her energy and she has not opened the app in two weeks. What should she try first?
choices: Recommit to the full ten minutes and use a guided session for accountability.
Take three slow breaths right after she sets the baby down for the first nap.
Wake up earlier so she has guaranteed quiet time before the baby is up.
questions.explanation: Three breaths fits the floor of her current life, so the practice keeps existing while her energy is at its worst. The full ten minutes ignores her sleep debt, and waking earlier steals from the only sleep she gets without changing the size of the behavior.

questions.prompt: A small business owner wants to learn Python after her 10-hour workdays, but she keeps closing the tutorial within two minutes of opening it. What rule actually fits the energy she has on a Tuesday evening?
choices: Block 45 minutes after dinner with her phone in another room.
Wait until weekends when she has bandwidth for a 2-hour session.
Type one line of code before she pours her evening tea.
questions.explanation: One line is small enough to survive a Tuesday she barely got through. Forty-five minute blocks size the behavior to a self she does not have on weekdays, and saving it for weekends abandons the daily practice she actually wanted to build.

questions.prompt: A middle school teacher wanted to write three gratitudes every night, but she keeps falling asleep right after grading. Two weeks in, she has written nothing. Which change best fits the matching principle?
choices: Shrink it to writing one word on the bedside notepad before plugging in her phone.
Move it to mornings when she is fresher and has more clarity.
Add a small reward like dark chocolate to make the writing feel attractive.
questions.explanation: One word fits the floor of her energy, so the practice survives the worst grading nights. Moving the time changes the cue but not the size, and a reward sweetens a behavior she still cannot reach when she is that exhausted.

questions.prompt: A rideshare driver tried drinking eight glasses of water daily for three weeks. He always forgot once the lunch rush hit, and he gave up. Which diagnosis best fits what actually went wrong?
choices: He lacked a strong enough reason; he needs to remember why hydration matters for long-term health.
He needed a tracking app to keep him honest and visualize his progress each day.
He sized the rule for an easy shift, not for the seven-hour back-to-back ride stretches that are normal for him.
questions.explanation: The pattern is sizing for the easy day and then blaming yourself on the hard one. Reasons and tracking apps both leave the original target in place, so the same gap reopens the next time the lunch rush kills his attention.

questions.prompt: A startup founder has tried journaling four separate times. Each plan starts on a calm Sunday and dies by Thursday. What does the recurring pattern most likely point to?
choices: He picked the wrong cue; journaling pairs better with morning coffee than with the end of the workday.
He planned for Sunday-night him, not the version of him who finishes a Thursday investor call at 11pm.
He never built a real celebration into the routine, and without that emotional payoff a habit cannot stick.
questions.explanation: The Sunday/Thursday gap is the diagnosis. He keeps writing the plan for a rested founder, and the tired one cannot execute it. Cue placement and celebration are real levers, but neither addresses the size-versus-floor mismatch driving the four failures.

questions.prompt: A retired engineer set a 500-word daily memoir goal. He hit it for three days, missed twelve in a row, and abandoned the project. Which read best explains the failure?
choices: He needs a stricter accountability partner who checks in on his word count daily.
Five hundred words is reasonable; he just needs to develop discipline through consistent practice.
Five hundred words was sized to his first-week enthusiasm, not the average tired afternoon. The rule never matched the floor of his motivation.
questions.explanation: First-week energy is not the average. A rule sized to that spike collapses the moment the spike ends. Accountability and discipline framings both assume the target is fine, which is the misread the matching principle exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: Two coworkers compare habit plans. He sets his morning runs based on his peak Saturday energy. She plans hers based on her worst Wednesday energy. Whose approach better matches the principle, and why?
choices: Hers, because a rule sized to her hardest day will still hold on her best one.
His, because aiming high pulls the behavior upward through aspiration.
Both work, since the principle stays neutral about which tide level you design for.
questions.explanation: The rule is only as strong as the day you keep it on. Designing for the worst day means it survives every other day too. Aspirational sizing buys a few good weeks and then a long quiet collapse, and treating the principle as neutral ignores why matching exists at all.

reviewCards.front: You keep abandoning a new habit on weeknights even though it goes fine on weekends. What is the actual failure mode this calls you to name?
reviewCards.back: You sized the behavior for your high-motivation self, not your low-motivation self. Match the behavior to the motivation you actually have on the worst night of the week, not the best. The fix is to shrink the behavior to fit the floor of your energy, not raise your willpower to meet the ceiling.

reviewCards.front: A friend tells you he wants to journal one paragraph after every late rehearsal, but he has skipped nine nights running. What single question should you put to him?
reviewCards.back: Ask what is the smallest version of this that tired-Wednesday you would still do. Then have him write that exact version down, even if it is one sentence on a sticky note. The point is to design the habit for the actual person putting the trumpet away at 9:47 p.m., not a fresh well-rested version of him.

reviewCards.front: You have ADHD and your motivation swings hour to hour. You are tempted to set one ambitious daily rule and just push through. What rule structure fits your real life better?
reviewCards.back: Write two sizes of the same behavior, one for high-motivation days and one for low-motivation days, and let both count as a win. One line on a bad morning, thirty minutes on a good one. The habit survives because the floor version is small enough to do on any day, so the streak never breaks.

reviewCards.front: A night-shift nurse wants to start stretching after twelve-hour shifts and keeps failing. She asks you to help her redesign. What reframing question moves her past willpower?
reviewCards.back: Ask what stretch she can do while the kettle boils at 3 a.m. The question shifts her from amplifying motivation she does not have to shrinking the behavior until it fits inside the energy she actually has at the end of a shift. Sizing to the real moment, not the imagined one, is the move.

reviewCards.front: Your partner is defending an ambitious plan to cook dinner together every weeknight. The schedules are mismatched and resentment is building. What should you ask out loud to redirect the conversation?
reviewCards.back: Ask what is the version of this we can do on the worst night of the week. The question forces both of you to design for the floor of your shared motivation instead of the ceiling, so the plan survives a bad Wednesday rather than collapsing the first time one of you is exhausted. You are matching the size of the behavior to the energy you actually have, together.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Sizing a behavior to the motivation you actually have on your worst day, not the version of you on your best day. You learn to scout the floor of your week, find the lowest-energy slot, and design the habit to fit there. Once it survives the floor, the ceiling takes care of itself.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to commit to a new daily work habit, then write down what tired-Wednesday-at-4pm you would still do, and make that the rule.
If you skip a workout three days in a row, then cut the routine to one stretch or one pushup and run that version until it sticks.
If you and your partner are arguing about an ambitious shared plan, then ask out loud what the worst-night version looks like and agree on that one first.
If you catch yourself planning a budgeting session for Sunday morning, then design a thirty-second version you can do Wednesday night after dinner instead.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one habit you have abandoned in the last six months. Tonight, write down the smallest version of it that takes under thirty seconds, and put a sticky note where you will see it tomorrow.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, sit down for five minutes and audit your active habits. For each one, ask whether tired-Wednesday you would still do it, and shrink any habit that fails that test before the next week starts.

memorableLines.text: You are not lazy. You are under-designed.
memorableLines.why: It reframes personal failure as a design problem instead of a willpower deficit—a surprising and apt inversion that stops readers cold.

memorableLines.text: He does not need to want it more. He needs to want it less, and to design for that.
memorableLines.why: This counterintuitive flip of the expected solution (want it more) to the actual lever (want it less) is the chapter's intellectual core compressed into one sentence.

memorableLines.text: From the floor, things grew, including the marriage.
memorableLines.why: The connection between tiny behavior design and relationship healing is unexpected—the final three words elevate habit technique into life transformation.

chapters.title: Ability-Easy Does It
chapters.hook: If a behavior feels hard, it is not too small yet, and the fix is almost never more grit.
chapters.counterintuition: Most readers assume the bottleneck on a stalled habit is time, and they keep negotiating with their calendar. It is usually one of five other things: money, physical effort, mental effort, routine fit, or social fit, and the wrong fix on the wrong bottleneck is why discipline keeps failing them.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Find which one of time, money, physical effort, mental effort, routine fit, or social fit is throttling the habit, then shrink the behavior at exactly that bottleneck.

breakdown.fastRead:
You bought the shoes. You set the alarm. You quit by Thursday. That is not a story about weakness. That is a story about a behavior that was too big for your real life.

A behavior happens when it is easy. If you can do it tired, distracted, in a bad mood, on a hard day, it sticks. If it only works when the stars line up, it dies on a Tuesday.

So shrink it. One pushup, not twenty. One sentence in the journal, not a page. Floss one tooth.

If it still feels hard, it is not small enough yet. Make it smaller. You are not lazy. You are under-designed.
breakdown.deepRead:
Picture a Sunday night. A bakery owner sits at the kitchen table with three weeks of receipts in a paper bag and a laptop he does not trust. He plans to enter all of it tonight. He won't. He hasn't for four months.

The story he tells himself is that he is bad with computers, or bad with money, or just lazy. None of it is true. The behavior, as designed, is impossible for the person he actually is on a Sunday night. Every week the receipts pile higher, and the shame of the bag gets heavier than the bag.

Ability has six bottlenecks. Time. Money. Physical effort. Mental effort. Routine fit. Social fit. A stalled habit is almost always being throttled by exactly one of them. Find which one. Cut there.

For the bakery owner, the bottleneck is mental effort. Reconciling weeks of receipts at 9pm takes focus he does not have left. Move the behavior to right after he locks the front door, and shrink it to tagging one transaction. He can do that. He has done it five hundred times. The first night he tags one and feels a small flicker of pride. That is the wiring happening.

A junior paralegal at a busy immigration firm has the same problem in a different shape. She wants to drink more water. Time is not the issue. Memory is not the issue. The bottleneck is the eight-step trip to the kitchen between back-to-back client intakes, where every step costs a client a minute, and a missed minute can mean a missed deadline. Move the bottle to her desk. The headaches retreat within a week.

The behavior that fits inside your real day is the one you do. Everything else is theater.
breakdown.fullRead:
It is Sunday at 9pm and you are staring at your running shoes by the door. You set an alarm for 6am. You picture the new version of yourself. Tomorrow evening, faced with the actual behavior in your actual life, you don't do it. You call it a willpower problem. You are wrong about why.

The lever you reach for is motivation, because motivation is the loudest part of behavior and the easiest to talk about. It is also the least reliable. Motivation is a tide. It is high on Monday morning and low on Thursday at 8pm, and you cannot build a house on it. The structural lever is ability. Make a behavior easy enough and it happens at low motivation. Leave it hard, and no amount of Monday hope carries you through Thursday at 8pm.

Ability splits into six dimensions, and a stalled habit is usually being squeezed by exactly one. How much it costs you in minutes. How much it costs you in dollars. How much your body has to do. How much your brain has to do. Whether it fits the rhythm of your day. Whether the people around you make it harder. Do not push harder against the wall. Figure out which wall, and walk around it.

Consider a freelance violist preparing for a regional audition while raising a toddler. She has the desire. She has the talent. She has, in any given week, twenty minutes of practice that arrives in chunks of three or four. The conventional advice, build up to ninety minutes a day, does not survive contact with her life. She tries it for a month and quits, and the audition date keeps coming. Miss it and she waits another year for the next one. Then she rewrites the rule. The practice is opening the case and playing one bar. Not as a warm-up. As the whole thing. Anything more is bonus, not assignment. The first night she plays for forty minutes, because the resistance was the threshold, not the work. The second night she plays for two minutes, because the toddler is teething. Both nights count. That is the design.

Now the part that catches people. You can shrink a behavior and still fail, and it is almost always because you shrunk along the wrong axis. A widowed retiree told to walk thirty minutes a day cuts it to fifteen, and still does not go. He cuts it to ten. Still nothing. Time was never the bottleneck. The bottleneck was the cost of leaving the house on a grief day, the weight of the front door. The version that works is putting on his shoes and stepping onto the porch. Anything past the porch is optional. On the days the porch is all he has, the porch counts. Most days, he walks twenty minutes anyway, because the porch was the door.

If a tiny behavior still feels hard, you have not made it small enough, or you have shrunk the wrong axis. Do not push. Diagnose. Find your actual constraint on a Tuesday night. Cut there. Design for your worst day, not your best one. The habit that survives your worst day is the only one you actually have.

examples.title: Sunita's 3 a.m. Stretch in the ICU Supply Closet

planSpec.domain: a night-shift ICU nurse trying to start a stretching habit between 3am rounds
planSpec.audience: a healthcare worker whose energy budget is already spent
planSpec.stakes: chronic lower-back pain that will end her bedside career within five years if she does not move
planSpec.requiredBeat: she identifies that mental effort, not time, is the bottleneck and cuts the habit from a ten-minute routine to a single hamstring stretch against the supply closet door

examples.scenario: Sunita is the charge nurse on a Tuesday night shift, standing in the supply closet at 3:08 a.m. between rounds. Her lower back is locked up again. She has a printed ten-minute stretching routine taped inside her locker, and she has not done it once in six weeks. The dog-eared paper is right there. Her badge is clipped, her pager is quiet for maybe ninety seconds. She is about to skip it again, telling herself she is too tired, when she catches the real reason: it is not the ten minutes, it is having to remember the ten moves in order while her brain is full of bed 4's potassium.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the routine to one hamstring stretch against the supply closet door. Do that one stretch every time you enter the closet. Nothing else counts, nothing else is required.
examples.whyItMatters: When mental effort is the binding constraint, shrinking time does not help. Removing the sequence to remember collapses the decision cost to zero, so the behavior can fire on a tired brain.

examples.title: Csilla, Eleven Days Out, Plays a Single Bar

planSpec.domain: a freelance violist preparing for a regional audition while raising a toddler
planSpec.audience: a working artist with fragmented practice time
planSpec.stakes: whether she keeps her chair in the orchestra or loses it to a younger player
planSpec.requiredBeat: she opens the case and plays one bar — not as a warm-up, but as the entire practice — and feels the resistance dissolve the moment she lets the bar count

examples.scenario: It is 9:47 p.m. and Csilla's toddler has finally surrendered to sleep in the next room. The audition is in eleven days. The viola case sits on the kitchen table next to a bowl of unrinsed grapes. She unlatches it, draws the bow, and plays the first bar of the Hindemith. Then she stops. That is practice tonight. One bar. She closes the case before the part of her that wants to play more can argue with the part of her that just did.
examples.whatToDo: Open the case, play one bar, and let that one bar count as the entire practice. Close the case before you negotiate yourself into doing more.
examples.whyItMatters: On a fragmented night the expensive part is not playing, it is starting. A version small enough to survive fatigue gets repeated, and the reps are what hold a chair in an orchestra, not heroic sessions.

examples.title: Florian's Lockup Tag Replaces His Sunday Receipt Pile

planSpec.domain: a regional bakery owner trying to learn bookkeeping software after years of paper ledgers
planSpec.audience: a small-business owner in his late fifties who has rejected three productivity systems
planSpec.stakes: a tax season he cannot afford to botch again
planSpec.requiredBeat: the before version asks him to reconcile a week of receipts on Sunday night; the after version is opening the app and tagging one transaction after he locks the front door

examples.scenario: Florian, who has run the Greenpoint bakery for twenty-three years, tried it the obvious way first: every Sunday at nine he poured a glass of wine, dumped a week of crumb-flecked receipts onto the kitchen table, and opened the bookkeeping app his accountant kept emailing him about. He did this twice, then quit. The new rule is different. After he turns the front-door key each night, before he walks to the car, he opens the app on his phone and tags one transaction. One. Then he goes home.
examples.whatToDo: Move the practice from Sunday-night reconciliation to a single tagged transaction at lockup. Cut the behavior until time, mental load, and routine fit all stop arguing with you.
examples.whyItMatters: Sunday-night batching stacks every bottleneck at once: tired, alone, facing a week of decisions. Lockup already happens every day. One tag takes ten seconds. Nothing in the design is fighting the behavior, so it actually runs.

examples.title: Esha and Niko Redesign the Cue at the Coffee Maker

planSpec.domain: a high school chemistry teacher and her partner negotiating who feeds the dog at 6am
planSpec.audience: a couple where one person carries most of the household's invisible labor
planSpec.stakes: a low-grade resentment that has started leaking into their weekends
planSpec.requiredBeat: they discover that the bottleneck is not willingness but routine fit — the partner's morning starts in a different room — and they redesign the cue around the coffee maker instead of the alarm

examples.scenario: Saturday, 8 a.m. Esha sets her mug down. 'You said you'd feed Mochi at six. Again it was me.' 'I want to,' Niko says. 'I just don't hear the alarm from the guest room.' 'So it isn't that you don't care.' 'I'm already in the kitchen by six fifteen, making coffee. The alarm goes off in a room I'm not in.' Esha is quiet. 'What if the cue isn't the alarm?' 'Go on.' 'What if the cue is the coffee maker. You scoop kibble while it brews.' Niko looks at the carafe, at the bag, then back.
examples.whatToDo: Move the cue out of the room where the behavior keeps failing and pin it to something the partner already does. The coffee maker, not the alarm, becomes the prompt for feeding the dog.
examples.whyItMatters: A prompt only fires if the person is in earshot of it. Willingness was never the variable; routine fit was. Anchoring the cue to a kitchen step the partner already takes puts the bowl in the path he already walks.

examples.title: Hector and the Porch That Becomes the Entire Route

planSpec.domain: a recently widowed retiree trying to walk daily after his cardiologist's warning
planSpec.audience: an older reader for whom 'just thirty minutes a day' has been useless advice
planSpec.stakes: a second cardiac event the doctor said was likely within eighteen months
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sets the rule that the walk is putting on his shoes and stepping onto the porch — anything beyond that is optional — and on a hard grief day discovers that this is the only version he can actually do

examples.scenario: Hector is sixty-eight, four months a widower. The cardiologist's number, eighteen months, is taped to the fridge under a peach-shaped magnet. His rule, written on an index card beside it, is one line: 'Shoes on. Step onto the porch.' Anything past that is optional. This Tuesday the bed feels like wet sand and her cardigan is still on the chair where she left it. He gets the shoes on. He gets to the porch. He sits on the cold top step and breathes. He does not go further. Today, that is the whole assignment, and it counts.
examples.whatToDo: Define the smallest version of the behavior that survives your worst day, then let that version count as the full assignment whenever it is all you can do.
examples.whyItMatters: A behavior that requires a good day is a behavior you will lose on a bad one. Sizing it for the worst day is the only way the repetition survives long enough to become a habit.

examples.title: Ngozi predicts the wrong bottleneck on her water habit

planSpec.domain: a junior immigration paralegal trying to drink more water during back-to-back client intakes
planSpec.audience: a young professional in a high-volume desk job
planSpec.stakes: recurring tension headaches that are starting to affect her case accuracy
planSpec.requiredBeat: the reader is asked to predict which constraint is binding before the answer is revealed — it is not time or memory but the physical effort of standing up, solved by moving the bottle from the kitchen to her desk

examples.scenario: Picture Ngozi, a junior immigration paralegal three intakes deep on a Tuesday, with a tension headache climbing the back of her skull. She has tried sticky notes on her monitor. She has tried a phone alarm every hour. Both failed. Before you read on, predict which constraint is binding for her: time, memory, or something else. Most readers guess memory. The honest answer is physical effort. Her water bottle lives in the office kitchen, two corridors away, and standing up between back-to-back clients costs her more than she has. Her hand is on the sticky note, ready to write a fourth reminder.
examples.whatToDo: Move the bottle from the kitchen to the corner of her desk, within arm's reach of her keyboard. Sip whenever a client pauses to gather a document.
examples.whyItMatters: The binding constraint was never attention or willingness. It was the dozen steps between her chair and the water. Shrinking distance shrinks effort, and effort is the lever that actually moves.

examples.title: Ravi rebuilds Wednesday dinners around a single onion

planSpec.domain: a divorced father re-learning to cook on the two nights a week his daughters stay over
planSpec.audience: a parent stitching a household back together one routine at a time
planSpec.stakes: whether his daughters experience these nights as a real home or a holding pattern
planSpec.requiredBeat: he notices that the bottleneck was never skill or time but the mental load of choosing a recipe, and the tiny version becomes 'chop one onion before the kettle boils' — a behavior small enough to survive a bad week

examples.scenario: Ravi is standing at the sink on a Wednesday night, water running over his hands, replaying why Tuesday went sideways again. It wasn't time. He had time. It wasn't skill. He can chop. What broke him, he sees now, was the twelve minutes he spent scrolling for a recipe before he even put the kettle on. By the time he picked one, the girls were hungry, he was tired, and the whole night tilted into takeout and apologies. The fix forms in his head like a small clean shape. Chop one onion before the kettle boils. That is the whole thing. Not dinner. An onion.
examples.whatToDo: Strip the cooking behavior to chopping one onion before the kettle finishes boiling. Skip recipe selection entirely. If a meal grows from there, fine. If not, the habit still ran tonight.
examples.whyItMatters: The binding constraint was decision load, not skill or minutes. A behavior anchored to a fixed cue and stripped of choosing survives the nights when energy collapses, because choosing is the expensive part.

questions.prompt: A copy editor wants to start a daily walk but has stopped after three weeks. She tells herself she lacks discipline. What is the most useful way to frame the problem?
choices: Her discipline is fine; one of six specific friction points (time, money, physical effort, mental effort, routine fit, or social fit) is throttling the behavior, and the next move is to find which one.
She needs a more ambitious goal so the walk feels meaningful enough to fight for.
She should track motivation each morning and only walk on days it crosses a threshold.
questions.explanation: Stalled behaviors are almost always throttled by one specific ability bottleneck, not by character. Naming the six lets you diagnose. Bigger goals raise motivation but worsen ability. Walking only when motivated guarantees collapse on hard days.

questions.prompt: A medical resident wants to start a five-minute morning meditation but keeps skipping it after thirty-hour shifts. What is the soundest next move?
choices: Set two alarms fifteen minutes apart so she is more likely to hear one and get out of bed.
Hold the five-minute target and start a thirty-day streak with a friend for accountability.
Cut the practice to one slow exhale before her feet hit the floor, with anything beyond that optional.
questions.explanation: If a behavior dies on hard days, it is too big. Shrinking to one breath fits a post-shift body and brain. More alarms do not fix ability. A streak commitment raises stakes without lowering the difficulty curve, which is the actual bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A new dad wants to do four-minute shoulder PT after rotator cuff surgery, but the elastic band lives in an upstairs closet while he spends most evenings downstairs with the baby. What is the best redesign?
choices: Hang the band on a hook beside the couch so the equipment is in arm's reach during baby downtime.
Block a non-negotiable nine pm slot on the calendar for PT, even if the baby has just gone down.
Watch a daily tutorial video so he stays motivated to climb the stairs and do the work.
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is physical friction: the band is fifteen steps from where his body actually is. Moving equipment to the body removes that friction. Calendars do not solve location friction. Tutorial videos boost motivation, which is not the reliable lever for ability problems.

questions.prompt: An accountant has been 'studying Italian for an hour after dinner' for two weeks before his family's Rome trip and has not opened the app once. He says he just needs to focus. What is the most useful redesign?
choices: Enroll in a thirty-day intensive course whose structure carries him through low-energy nights.
Make the habit 'open the app and tap one flashcard' the moment he sets down his fork, with more being optional.
Block social media on his phone after eight pm so distractions cannot steal the hour.
questions.explanation: An hour of evening study is too big for his actual energy budget. Shrinking to one tap and anchoring to a moment that already happens makes it doable on any night. Intensive courses raise difficulty. Distraction blockers do not change the size of the behavior.

questions.prompt: A property manager wants to do a fifteen-minute evening stretch after work but keeps collapsing on the couch instead. She has floor space and time. What is the right diagnosis and fix?
choices: Time is the bottleneck; wake twenty minutes earlier and do the routine before the workday.
Mental effort after a long day is the bottleneck; shrink to one stretch the moment she walks in, before she sits down.
Motivation is the bottleneck; tape a photo of her chiropractor's bill to the fridge.
questions.explanation: She has time and space. What she lacks at six pm is the cognitive bandwidth for a fifteen-minute routine. Shrinking to one stretch right at the door beats sitting down first. Earlier alarms add a different kind of cost. Guilt photos pull on motivation, which fluctuates.

questions.prompt: A pediatric dentist wants to journal each evening but only manages it about once a week. She is not tired. The notebook is by the bed. She stares at the blank page and ends up scrolling instead. Which bottleneck best fits?
choices: Physical effort: picking up the notebook is more friction than picking up the phone.
Routine fit: bedtime is the wrong slot for a reflective habit.
Mental effort: a blank page demands cognitive work she does not have at end of day.
questions.explanation: She has access, time, and a slot, so location and routine are not the issue. What stalls her is the open-ended cognitive load of inventing what to write. Shrinking the prompt to one bullet ('one moment from today') would address it directly.

questions.prompt: A construction estimator and his husband want to start a shared evening walk, but the estimator's workday ends at seven pm while the husband eats dinner at five thirty. They keep arguing about scheduling. What is actually broken?
choices: Social fit: one partner does not really want to walk and is using time as an excuse.
Routine fit: their evening rhythms do not overlap, so the cue has nowhere stable to live.
Physical effort: a post-work walk is too demanding for the estimator's energy.
questions.explanation: Both want to walk and both can physically do it. The constraint is that their existing routines do not share an anchor moment, so no reliable cue exists. Calling it social fit misreads willingness as the problem; calling it physical effort ignores their stated energy.

questions.prompt: A high-end caterer wants to prep the next day's mise en place each night. She has the time, the kitchen is already clean, and her body is fine. But staring at tomorrow's menu at ten pm, she freezes and walks away. Which framing best names the binding constraint?
choices: Physical effort: her body is too tired after service to chop, even though she says otherwise.
Routine fit: ten pm is too late in the night for any productive work.
Mental effort, in the form of choice load: deciding what to prep is the part that is too heavy.
questions.explanation: She is not stalled on chopping; she is stalled on choosing. That is mental effort showing up as choice paralysis. The fix is to remove the choice (a fixed nightly task like 'chop the onions for tomorrow's first dish'). Body fatigue and clock time are not what she actually reports.

questions.prompt: A bus driver wants to start strength training at home. He is choosing among three starter versions. Which design is the strongest?
choices: After taking off his work boots, he does one squat next to the boot rack. Anything more is a bonus.
After dinner, he does the shortest beginner workout video he can find, around twelve minutes.
Three nights a week he does a real workout when he has energy, prioritizing consistency over volume.
questions.explanation: The first option ties to a fixed daily anchor and shrinks the behavior to something doable on his worst day. A twelve-minute video is still too big for tired nights. The 'when I have energy' rule outsources the call to motivation, which fades exactly when he needs it.

questions.prompt: A grant writer cannot keep up his 'review one foundation's funding priorities each morning' habit. He blames focus. On closer look, he opens the database, sees seventeen saved-search tabs, and bounces. Which response best fits the actual problem?
choices: Hire a productivity coach to fix his focus, since the database mess is just a symptom.
Block forty-five minutes on his calendar so he can do the review uninterrupted and properly.
Pin one foundation's URL and redefine the habit as 'open that one tab and read the top line.'
questions.explanation: Seventeen tabs is choice load disguised as a focus problem. Reducing to one pinned tab cuts the mental effort to near zero. Coaching does not change the design. A bigger calendar block makes the behavior larger, which is the opposite of what a stalled habit needs.

reviewCards.front: You wanted to journal every night and have skipped it for two weeks. Before blaming your discipline, what is the first question this framework tells you to ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask which of the six ability bottlenecks is throttling the behavior: time, money, physical effort, mental effort, routine fit, or social fit. A stalled habit is almost always choked by exactly one of them, so name that one before redesigning anything else.

reviewCards.front: A friend says she keeps meaning to stretch after night shifts at the hospital but cannot make herself do a ten minute routine at 3am. What move does this call for?
reviewCards.back: Cut the behavior to its smallest meaningful version that attacks the real bottleneck. If mental effort is what she lacks at 3am, the habit becomes one hamstring stretch against the nearest door. Anything more is optional, not the assignment.

reviewCards.front: You and your partner keep fighting about who feeds the dog at 6am. You both want to help. What bottleneck should you suspect, and what does the fix look like?
reviewCards.back: Suspect routine fit, not willingness. The cue is probably anchored to a routine one of you does not actually pass through. Move the prompt to a routine the willing partner already does, like starting the coffee maker, instead of leaning on the alarm.

reviewCards.front: A small business owner has tried three productivity systems for bookkeeping and quit each one. He blames himself. How would you redesign his Sunday night reconciliation session?
